p: `source = "abc"`, `target = "abcbc"`:

Taking as many target letters as possible from each copy of `source` never hurts, because any leftover is the same suffix problem on a shorter target. Matching a letter earlier in the pass than necessary only leaves later letters for the next ones.

For many queries, precompute for each position and letter where the next occurrence is in `source`, or keep sorted position lists per letter and binary search them. That gives O(|target| log |source|) per query.

1055.takeaway: Shortest way to form a string: greedily match as much of the target as possible in each pass over the source; a pass with no progress means impossible.

blocks.h: Why is the answer a suffix?
p: Among all substrings starting at a position, the longest one starting there is lexicographically largest (a prefix is smaller than the longer string). So the largest substring overall is the largest SUFFIX, and the problem reduces to comparing suffixes.

Each comparison step either extends `k` or moves `i` or `j` forward by `k + 1`. The pointers only move forward and `i + j + k` grows, so the total work is linear even though characters are re-compared after a skip.

1163.takeaway: Last substring in lexicographic order = the maximum suffix, found with two candidates and a skip rule in O(n).
